title: Invisible Users, Invisible Interfaces: Accelerating Design Iteration with AI Simulation - Alex Liss

summary: Alex Liss, VP of Data Science and AI at Huge design and technology company, addresses the current state of UX and AI through three lenses: where we are, where we could be, and how to get there. He identifies an AI trust gap, citing Edelman research from December 2024 showing only 32% of US adults and 44% of adults globally trust AI, attributing this to AI slop—instances where generative AI produces obviously incorrect outputs. He argues the real genAI opportunity is not bolting chatbots onto websites but leveraging natural language interaction as a UX revolution, returning to Don Norman's principle of invisible interfaces that feel seamless and intuitive. Liss proposes an AI-accelerated needfinding process that parallels traditional design lifecycle steps—defining audiences, mapping intentions, identifying tasks, conducting analysis, refining insights, and developing design alternatives—but introduces Intelligent Twins as simulated user personas built on Huge's Live data platform. These twins combine demographic, psychographic, and contextual data to represent user behaviors, needs, and motivations, then evaluate interfaces through task-based briefings similar to heuristic analysis. He demonstrates the methodology through a global sports website audit across basketball, Olympics, and English Premier League sites, using two personas (casual fan and super fan) across three task categories (navigation, information architecture, fan engagement) with four tasks each, yielding 72 simulated AI actions. Findings showed navigation performed well across leagues but success dropped as users moved deeper into browsing and engagement pathways. The methodology combines computer use models, computer vision, and human-in-the-loop observation to generate focused design briefs. Looking forward, he notes Anthropic's MCP protocol showing potential to convert Figma prototypes into React or Node.js components, emphasizing that as design creation gets easier, focusing on the why and strategy becomes more critical. He acknowledges limitations around reproducibility, standardization, and the need for test-and-control validation, and concludes that AI simulation can help repair the trust gap by enabling smarter, faster design processes.

sections.title: Introduction and the AI Trust Gap
sections.summary: Alex Liss introduces himself and outlines the three-part talk structure. He presents the current AI trust gap using Edelman research showing only 32% of US adults trust AI, attributing this to AI slop—obviously incorrect genAI outputs like suggesting eating rocks or buying a car for $1.

sections.title: UX First Principles and Invisible Interfaces
sections.summary: Liss argues the real genAI magic is natural language interaction with ML models, a UX revolution. He references Don Norman's principles of invisible interfaces—software so seamless users forget they're using it—and proposes using AI to accelerate needfinding rather than stuffing chatbots into websites.

sections.title: AI-Accelerated Needfinding Process
sections.summary: Liss compares the design process to pilot training through simulation. He outlines how the traditional needfinding lifecycle—defining audiences, mapping intentions, identifying tasks, analysis, refining insights, developing alternatives—can be enhanced with AI simulation, turning data artifacts into active participants.

sections.title: Intelligent Twins and the Live Data Platform
sections.summary: Huge's Live data platform provides demographic, psychographic, and contextual data to simulate audience behaviors. Intelligent Twins represent user behaviors, needs, and motivations, and can be briefed to evaluate interfaces through specific tasks, similar to briefing a human designer for heuristic analysis.

sections.title: Global Sports Website Audit Demonstration
sections.summary: Liss demonstrates the methodology through a global audit of sports websites (basketball, Olympics, English Premier League) using two personas—casual fan and super fan—across three task categories with four tasks each, generating 72 simulated AI actions. Navigation performed well but success dropped deeper into browsing and engagement.

sections.title: Generating Design Briefs and Future Outlook
sections.summary: The methodology combines computer use models, computer vision, and human-in-the-loop observation to generate focused design briefs. Liss notes Anthropic's MCP protocol showing potential to convert Figma prototypes into code components, emphasizing strategy becomes more critical as creation tools accelerate.

sections.title: Limitations and Conclusion
sections.summary: Liss acknowledges limitations including reproducibility, standardization needs, and test-and-control validation. He concludes that users don't need more broken chatbot features but better interfaces, and AI simulation can help design teams gather insights smarter and faster to repair the trust gap.
